To be or not to be, is that still the question?

The topic of AI sovereignty has been in the news a lot lately. Back in June Trump demanded Anthropic and OpenAI put restrictions on distributions of models to the EU. Although not the origin of the European “digital sovereignty” discussions it was definitively an acceleration point. As is the nature of bureaucracy, the powers that be had already spent many meetings doing a lot of talking, and talking, and talking, with little forward traction. Trump’s tantrum forced the conversation to move forward, somehow. Coincidentally, at the same time that the Trump administration was putting together their directive to prevent the use of Fable 5 and Mythos 5 by foreign nationals the EU was unveiling their latest tech sovereignty package, including the announcement of Mistral’s Compute strategy. This may seem to many like a nothing burger, this emerging picture has made for some interesting conversations. On one hand the argument that moving away from the EU’s reliance on foreign tech is a step in the right direction, on the other hand EU tech is behind and catching up will take a collective European mind shift.

To be or not to be, is that still the question?

AI sovereignty is in the news now.

It also announced Mistral’s Compute strategy.

Some see moving away from foreign tech as good for the EU.

Others think EU tech is behind and will need a big mindset change.

output_text_len:
Digital technologies spread information faster.  

They connect people worldwide.  

These tools give us lots of knowledge.  

But they can cause information overload.  

We need good filters to tell truth from lies.
